lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Braulio Zemel | Lesson 11 -- The Art of Storytelling
lesson.grammar_point: used to, be used to and get used to

listenings.text: So this happened about ten years ago, and I still cannot explain it. I used to take the same train home every evening, the six forty, and there was always the same man in the third carriage reading the same enormous book. Every day, for about a year. I got used to seeing him there. Then one Thursday he was not on the train, and I noticed, which surprised me, because I had never spoken a word to him. Two weeks later I was in a bookshop on the other side of the city and there he was, behind the counter. And the book he had been reading for a year on that train was a dictionary. Not a novel with a dull cover. An actual dictionary. I asked him about it, obviously, and he said he had been learning Portuguese, one page a day, because his wife was Brazilian and he had got tired of not understanding her family.

There are three things that separate a story from an event, and none of them is vocabulary. The first is that a story has a shape, and the shape is short. Set the scene in one sentence, not four. Where, when, and who. The second is that something has to turn. If nothing turns, you have described a Tuesday, and people are polite about descriptions of Tuesdays but they do not remember them. The third is the ending, and this is where most people go wrong in a second language, because they keep talking after the story has finished. The turn is the end. Say it and stop. If you have to explain what the story meant, the story did not work, and explaining it will not repair it. One more thing that helps enormously. Tell the same story three times to three different people in the same week. By the third time you will have found the shape without trying, and you will notice you have cut about a third of the words.

extra_audio.text: Sylvia asks Braulio whether he has a story from the month he spent in San Francisco. He tells her that he used to rent a room in a family house on purpose, so that he would have to speak English at breakfast. Sylvia asks him whether it worked. He answers that for three weeks he understood almost nothing, and then one morning he realized he had been following the whole conversation without noticing. Sylvia tells him that is the whole story, and that he should stop there instead of explaining it.
